runs.latest_final:
The man was being extorted: an unavoidable situation forced him to deliver a ransom payment, with a hostage to be released in exchange. The extortionists named a sum substantially larger than one million yen, and he intended the one million yen to be part of that payment.

He feared for his own safety because of what the bag would be seen to contain. He worried that if the criminals discovered the bag held precisely one million yen—short of what they demanded—the deception would fail and they would turn on him. So he added more of his own cash to the bag, making its total exceed one million yen while it remained less than the full demanded amount.

The point of the added cash was to deceive the extortionists into believing they had received the entire amount they demanded. With the larger pile of cash, he hoped that at the handover they would look at the thick bundle, assume the demand had been satisfied, and not carefully count or scrutinize it; the shortfall would not be noticed until it was too late. That mistaken belief was what he wanted in order to protect himself and get through the exchange.

The money—including the extra cash he had contributed—was handed over and kept by the extortionists; he never expected to recover it. He was deliberately sacrificing a larger sum than the one million yen in order to create the appearance that the full demand had been met, thereby protecting himself from the extortionists.

The man receiving the call is the daughter's father, but the daughter is not the hostage and is not necessarily even the caller in the usual sense. The hostage is a relative of the daughter—established as "yes"—while not being her husband, son, daughter, mother, or sibling, and also not the father's wife, parent, grandchild, sibling, friend, neighbor, or pet. The father himself is simultaneously being held captive by the same kidnapper who makes the demand, although he is not jailed and is not merely metaphorically trapped. He is able to arrange payment, and the captor knows he is on the phone. The hostage is not already dead, not a criminal, not a fake or staged victim, and not someone whose death would benefit the father. The father does not refuse because he lacks money, distrusts the demand as a hoax, wants police involvement, wishes to punish the hostage, or hopes to provoke a killing.

The key causal point supported by the evidence is that paying would not save the hostage and would instead strengthen the captor who is already holding the father. The father therefore concludes that the ransom should not be paid: the money would benefit the kidnapper, prolong the captivity, and—given the kidnapper's threat—would not reliably spare the hostage once the captor had the money. His refusal is a calculated response to being himself a captive and to believing that payment would worsen, rather than resolve, the situation.

runs.latest_final:
The situation was a real kidnapping with a twist: the person the kidnapper threatened to kill was not the daughter but her loved one. The kidnapper contacted the daughter, who was elsewhere, demanding she bring one hundred million yen alone by noon the next day, with no police, or the hostage would die. The daughter—who did have access to the money—was pleading over the phone to spare the hostage's life, and her father was also on the line, able to hear and speak.

The father decided the ransom should not be paid because of what paying would mean for his daughter's own life. To pay, the daughter would have to travel alone, without police, and put both herself and the money directly into the kidnapper's hands at the handover. The father concluded that such a meeting would be lethal to her: once she was there alone with the cash, the kidnapper would take the money and kill her, since nothing—no police, no witness, no protection—would restrain him. In his judgment, paying would therefore deliver his daughter to her death rather than secure anyone's safety.

By refusing to pay, he kept his daughter from ever going to that fatal handover, and that is precisely what would spare her life. He was willing to accept the terrible risk that the hostage—his daughter's loved one—might die, and he had no guarantee that paying would even save the hostage, because the kidnapper might kill the hostage anyway. Faced with that, he put his own daughter's survival first. The demand was thus a trap in which compliance would cost him his daughter, so he concluded the ransom should not be paid.

runs.latest_final:
The father is himself a hostage. At the time of the call he is locked away by captors who are holding him for ransom, so he cannot travel, cannot bring money "alone," and cannot reach his daughter by the noon deadline. The daughter is genuinely in the hands of a kidnapper who is threatening to kill her.

The father concludes the ransom should not be paid because, in his judgment, payment would lead to the daughter's death rather than her release, while withholding payment at least leaves her a chance to survive. Paying is not a safe route: he cannot deliver the money himself because he is confined, and any payment made cannot be trusted to end with her being released unharmed—once the kidnapper has his money, the daughter, who could identify him, is in the gravest danger. So even setting aside that he is physically unable to comply, the father decides the correct choice is to refuse the demand, keeping the daughter alive as a hostage rather than handing over a ransom that would not save her and would only make her expendable.

Thus the tragedy is twofold: a father who genuinely wants his daughter spared decides against paying because paying would not spare her, and he is powerless to act anyway—he is a captive himself, unable to deliver the hundred million yen alone by noon.

The father understood that the bear had not hunted or killed a living person; it had merely found and consumed a buried body left in bear country. The father is being held captive by a kidnapper. The kidnapper has him overhear (or be present for) a smartphone call in which the kidnapper demands that the daughter bring one hundred million yen, alone, by noon tomorrow—or the hostage, her father, will die—and warns her not to involve the police. Over the phone, the daughter begs the kidnapper to spare her father's life.

During the call, the father realizes the real trap: to deliver the money alone, his daughter would have to come to the kidnapper in person, and the kidnapper intends to harm or kill her at that handoff (to eliminate a witness). He is able to speak on the call, and he tells his daughter that the ransom should not be paid—his decision is meant to protect her. He understands that the kidnapper may well kill him whether or not the money is paid, and he accepts that risk rather than let his daughter walk into danger. The reason he refuses to let the ransom be paid is to keep his daughter from coming to the kidnapper and being killed.

runs.latest_final:
The father is himself the captive. The person on the phone begging for a life to be spared is his daughter, and she is begging for HIS life, not her own. She is free and elsewhere, calling because she loves him.

The kidnapper, holding the father, shouts the demand—one hundred million yen brought alone by noon tomorrow, or the hostage dies, no police. But the person being told to bring the money alone is the daughter. The father realizes what the demand actually means: it is a way to bring his daughter to the kidnapper's location.

The father, from his position as hostage, can still speak to her on the call, and he tells her not to pay and not to come. His refusal is not about saving himself—he knows paying will not save him—but a self-sacrifice: he would rather the kidnapper kill him than have his daughter deliver the money alone and place herself in danger on his behalf. He loves her and puts her safety above his own life, so the ransom should not be paid.
